info.ked_hv: HV: the radar sends a flat wave and listens for a twisted one. Gets brighter as leaves and stems grow.

sure.title: How sure are we?
sure.tagline: What radar does well, where it struggles, and what this is.
sure.agreement.pending: Agreement scores are computed at the event by comparing our maps with NASA's water maps. Each will show a range and a one-line meaning.
sure.f1.gloss: How well the two maps agree on where water is: 0 = not at all, 1 = perfectly.
sure.iou.gloss: Of all the places either map calls water, the share both agree on. Europe's Copernicus flood service aims for 0.70 or more.
sure.kappa.gloss: Agreement, after allowing for matches that would happen by chance.
sure.offset.gloss: Days between our radar picture and NASA's.
sure.benchmark: For scale: NASA's goal for NISAR is to map flooded areas with 80% accuracy, down to 1 ha, every 12 days. That is NASA's target, not something we have shown.
sure.values.title: Typical radar values
sure.values.tagline: Each number has a source, or is measured from our own radar pictures.
values.water.vv: Very dark: −15.5 dB or below (the limit used by NASA's HydroSAR tool)
values.water.vh: Very dark: −23 dB or below (same tool)
lim.provisional: Early data. NISAR pictures before 21 Oct 2026 are 'provisional': calibrated, but only checked at a few places, none in Southeast Asia. NASA's checked ('validated') data starts on 21 Oct 2026. Treat every number as an estimate.
lim.revisit.ked: Gaps between pictures. NISAR sees each strip of land every 12 days, so short floods can be missed. There are no NISAR pictures from 27 Jul to 10 Aug 2026.
lim.revisit.kel: Gaps between pictures. In late 2024 only one Sentinel-1 satellite was working, so Kelantan was seen only about every 6 days.
lim.nonisarflood: NISAR has not seen a flood here yet. It started in mid-2026, after the 2024 Kelantan flood, so that flood is shown with Sentinel-1 radar instead.
lim.blind.kel: Radar blind spots. Radar can mistake smooth roads, sand or shadows for water. It can miss water in towns, where flooded streets can look bright, and under thick trees. Wind and rain can roughen water so it looks like land.
lim.blind.ked: Radar blind spots. Radar can mistake smooth, dry soil or shadows for water. Wind and rain can roughen water so it looks like land.
lim.schedule: Planting dates. These come from a MADA notice. Real dates can differ field by field, especially in the 2026 drought year. The schedule is a plan, not what we observed.
lim.choices.kel: Our choices. We call a spot water if it is darker than −15.5 dB, the limit used by NASA's HydroSAR tool (our automatic method suggested a higher value on every date). Moving the limit 1 dB lower gives the low end of the range. We don't remove hill slopes and we leave towns out, so our flood areas are more likely too small than too big.
lim.choices.ked: Our choices. For each NISAR viewing path we picked the water limit automatically (Otsu's method) on the date where wet and dry fields were easiest to tell apart, and used it for every date. Moving the limits 1 dB either way gives the range shown. 'Rice land' means cropland on ESA's WorldCover 2021 map.
lim.notwarning: Not a warning service. This is not an official warning. For live river levels see Public InfoBanjir (JPS). For evacuation follow NADMA, JKM and APM instructions.
lim.notwarning.short: Not a warning service. Check MADA for planting advice.
lim.notreviewed: Not checked by experts. This is a student hackathon project using NASA data. NASA and outside scientists have not reviewed or endorsed it.
lim.passdays: Radar only on pass days. We only have radar pictures for days the satellite flew over. We don't guess the days in between.
lim.imagery: Pictures only. 'Anywhere' shows NASA's ready-made radar pictures. They are not measurements, early NISAR pictures are provisional, and different kinds of land can look alike.
lim.falsealarm.kel: False alarms and misses. Floods can be missed in towns, under thick trees, or when wind or heavy rain roughens the water. Smooth roads and sand can be wrongly marked as water.
lim.falsealarm.ked: False alarms and misses. Europe's Copernicus flood service warns that farmland can look like flood water to radar. In Kedah that is partly what we want to see, but smooth dry soil can look wet too.

story.1.title: Radar sees through cloud
story.1.body: During the monsoon, Kelantan can be under cloud for days. Radar satellites bring their own signal, so they see the ground anyway.
story.2.title: 17 November 2024: before
story.2.body: A normal radar view of the Kelantan delta. Rivers and lakes are dark because calm water reflects the signal away.
story.3.title: 29 November 2024: the flood
story.3.body: Twelve days later, as the flood rose toward its peak, large areas filled with water. Drag the slider to compare the two dates.
story.4.title: Where it hit
story.4.body: Our radar map counts new flood water in each district. Click a row to see where it hit. On 29 Nov, Pasir Mas and Tumpat had the most people in relief centres.
story.5.title: Kedah: NISAR watches fields fill
story.5.bridge: Same radar physics: dark = smooth water. In Kelantan it showed a disaster. In Kedah it shows farmers at work.
story.5.body: NISAR's longer radar waves (L-band) looked at Kedah's rice fields every few days from 23 September to 1 November 2026.
story.6.title: How sure are we?
story.6.body: We compare our maps with NASA's own water maps. In Kedah, NASA's map comes from a different radar, so it is a real check. In Kelantan both use the same radar, so it only shows we are consistent. NASA has not reviewed this project.
story.6.global: NISAR scans nearly all of Earth's land twice every 12 days, so this works far beyond Malaysia.
hint.tap: Click anywhere on the map to see what the radar saw.
about.title: About the data
about.tagline: Where every picture and number comes from.
about.passdays.title: Why only some days have radar
about.passdays.body: A radar satellite does not watch one place all the time. It takes a picture of a strip of ground as it flies over, and comes back to the same strip on the same path every 12 days. In late 2024 only one Sentinel-1 satellite was working, and it crossed Kelantan on two paths, so the area was seen about every 6 days. Between 17 and 29 November 2024 there are only three radar pictures: 17, 24 (early morning) and 29 November. On the other days there is simply no radar picture. We do not fill the gaps with guesses.
about.challenge.title: The challenge asks… our answer
about.why.a: Kelantan: heavy monsoon rain sets off the flood, the flat, low land spreads it, and high tides slow the water draining to the sea. Kedah: farmers flood their fields on a schedule set by dam water and rain. In 2026, drought pushed that schedule back.
about.pol.a: HH for open water, and for water under trees, buildings or young rice. HV for growing crops and trees. Sentinel-1's VV and VH channels do the same jobs with shorter waves.
about.future.a: Flood maps for disaster teams every 12 days, a planting tracker for MADA, and irrigation checks in dry years, for any river or rice area NISAR covers.
about.credits.title: Data and credits

about.ai.title: How AI was used
about.ai.body: This app was written with Claude Code (Anthropic). The AI analysis notes for each focus district were written by Claude on 14 Nov 2026 from our own radar results and NASA rainfall data. A script (pipeline/11_ai_analysis.py) checks that every number in them matches our results files. No person has reviewed them yet. No AI runs inside the page. All AI use is listed in AI_USAGE.md.

gloss.sar: SAR: a satellite radar that sends microwave pulses sideways and records the echoes. Works day or night, through cloud.
gloss.backscatter: Backscatter: the part of the radar signal that bounces back. Weak = dark pixel; strong = bright pixel.
gloss.hhhv: HH / HV: first letter = sent, second = received. HH shows water best; HV shows plants.
gloss.band: L-band / C-band: NISAR's 24 cm waves reach deeper into plants than Sentinel-1's ~5.5 cm waves.
gloss.pass: Pass day: a day the satellite flew over and took a radar picture.
gloss.track: Track: the repeating path of a satellite pass. Same-track pairs compare fairly.

explain.title: How radar sees water
explain.tagline: Four kinds of echo explain the colours on this map.
explain.mirror.title: Calm water is a mirror.
explain.mirror.body: The wave glances off away from the satellite, so almost nothing returns. Water looks dark in every channel.
explain.rough.title: Rough ground and choppy water.
explain.rough.body: The wave scatters in all directions and some comes back. VV and HH show this best. Wind or rain on water makes it brighter, which can hide a flood.
explain.volume.title: Leaves and branches.
explain.volume.body: The wave bounces around inside the canopy and comes back twisted. Cross-pol (HV, VH) rises as crops and trees grow.
explain.double.title: Double bounce.
explain.double.body: Water, then a wall, trunk or rice stem, sends the wave straight back. HH is brightest here, so flooded forest, flooded towns and young paddy can look bright, not dark.
explain.c: Sentinel-1 (about 5.5 cm): the Kelantan flood and NASA OPERA maps. Mostly sees the top of plants.
explain.s: NISAR's second radar (ISRO, about 10 cm). Not used here.
explain.l: NISAR (about 24 cm): Kedah's paddies. Reaches stems and trunks, so it sees water under plants better.

sure.agreement.kel: Scored on land only. At the flood peak, 29 Nov 2024, our map and NASA's agree with F1 {f1} and IoU {iou} (1 = perfect match). On dry dates there is little water on land, so a few river edges decide the score and it is low. The sea is left out because storm waves on 29 Nov made it look bright to the radar.
sure.agreement.ked: NISAR finds far more water in the fields than NASA's Sentinel-1 map. Almost all of NASA's water is inside ours, but most of ours is not in NASA's. Either NISAR's longer waves see shallow field water that Sentinel-1 misses, or smooth ploughed soil looks like water to NISAR. Without checks on the ground we can't tell which. See the layer 'Where NISAR and Sentinel-1 disagree'.

num.kel.chart.explain: How much new flood water our radar found on each date. It jumps to a peak on 29 Nov 2024, then falls as the water drains away.
num.kel.rank.explain: Which districts had the most new flood water on this date. A longer bar means more flooded land.
num.kel.rank.note: Big districts can show more hectares just because they are big. The AI analysis also compares them as a share of each district.
num.ked.chart.explain: The share of rice land with water in the fields on each radar date. It climbs as farmers flood their fields for planting, mostly in October.
num.ked.first.explain: When each field first got water. The tallest bar shows when most fields were flooded for planting.
rain.chart.explain: How much rain fell each day. Markers show the days the radar took a picture, so you can see how soon water appeared after heavy rain.
rain.chart.note: Click a bar to jump to the nearest radar picture.
sure.hist.kel.explain: Each curve shows how much of the land looked dark or bright to the radar. Anything darker than the dashed line counts as water.
sure.hist.ked.explain: Each curve shows how much of the rice land looked dark or bright. Fields darker than the dashed line count as wet.
layer.kel_duration: How long the water stayed (our map)
info.kel_duration: For every spot, the number of radar passes (6 days apart) on which our map showed new flood water. Seen on 2 passes means the water stayed about a week or more; on 3 or more, about two weeks or more.
kel.class.dur2: Seen on 2 passes (about a week or more)

impact.title: People and lasting water
impact.tagline: Who lived near the flood, and where the water stayed longest.
impact.people: About {n} people lived within {m} m of new flood water on {date}.
impact.people.in: About {n} of them lived right where our map shows water.
impact.people.compare: For scale: the news counted 65,993 people in relief centres across the whole of Kelantan that day. Not everyone near flood water had to leave home, so the two numbers measure different things.
impact.dur.title: Where the water stayed longest
impact.dur.explain: Land our radar saw under new flood water on two or more passes, {days} days apart. These places stayed flooded for about a week or more.
impact.dur.sub: Hectares seen flooded on 2 or more passes, by study district ({ha} in all)
impact.dur.note: Water that stays longer usually does more damage to homes and crops and slows recovery. Click a district to zoom to it.
impact.method: People: {src}, moved onto our 30 m grid. We count people living inside new flood water and within {m} m of it, because homes often sit on slightly higher ground beside flooded fields. This estimates who was close to the water; it is not a count of victims.
credit.worldpop: Population: WorldPop (www.worldpop.org), University of Southampton, Malaysia 2024 constrained population, 100 m, release R2025A (CC BY 4.0).
spot.title: This spot, radar pass by radar pass
spot.explain.kel: How bright the radar echo was here on every pass. When it drops below the dashed line, the spot looks like water.
spot.explain.ked: How bright the radar echo was here on every NISAR pass. HH drops when the field is flooded; HV rises as the rice grows.
spot.note.kel: Filled squares mark passes where our map shows new flood water here; hollow squares, none. Values are read from the map pictures (about ±0.3 dB).
spot.note.ked: Filled squares mark passes where our map found water in this field (HH and HV both below that path's water limits, after smoothing out speckle over neighbouring pixels, so a single reading near the limit can differ). NISAR looks from two angles on alternate passes, so the lines can zig-zag.
